articleHeadline: Bianca Andrade Reveals Diagnosis After Infection and Issues a Warning.
articleSummary: Bi Bianca Andrade, 31, was hospitalized in Brazil with pyelonephritis, a kidney infection that followed a urinary tract infection. There were no typical urinary symptoms early on, delaying diagnosis and allowing bacteria to ascend to the kidneys. Worsening back pain, persistent high fever, and imaging and blood tests confirmed pyelonephritis. Andrade warns that atypical infections can spread to the bloodstream and cause sepsis with multi-organ complications, underscoring the need for prompt medical evaluation with persistent symptoms. She cites conversations with friend Juliette and notes that actress Carolina Dieckmann was diagnosed with pyelonephritis in June, reporting ~39°C fever and back pain without classic urinary signs. Pyelonephritis is commonly caused by bacteria such as Escherichia coli; treatment involves antibiotics and hydration. This highlights importance of recognizing atypical presentations and seeking care in Brazil.

articleHeadline: Avian influenza in El Salvador: Is it dangerous to eat chicken? An infectious disease specialist clarifies doubts and warns about risks for agricultural workers.
articleSummary: El Salvador has issued a sanitary alert for Avian influenza, warning that while the disease mainly affects birds, it can pose health risks for people in contact with infected poultry. The Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock (MAG) declared the alert amid rising outbreaks across the Americas and prior human infections in neighboring countries. Avian influenza is caused by Influenza A viruses circulating among wild and domestic birds. The World Health Organization notes that humans can be infected through direct contact with ill animals during handling, slaughter, or processing, or via contaminated environments; indirect contact with contaminated surfaces also poses risk. Infectious disease specialist Jorge Panameño says there is no direct threat to El Salvador's public health at present, but poultry workers face real exposure risk. Symptoms range from fever and myalgia to cough and acute respiratory illness, with some asymptomatic cases; sustained human-to-human transmission has not been demonstrated. Since Oct 2025, outbreaks have been reported in the United States, Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Honduras, Costa Rica, and Colombia. El Salvador has strengthened surveillance in farms, markets, and border controls, and authorities urge vigilance.

articleHeadline: Streptococcosis control requires more than vaccination in tilapia production.
articleSummary: 520 tilapia vaccinated survey shows low detection of Streptococcus agalactiae serotype Ib, yet outcomes hinge on diagnosis, water quality, stress, and matching vaccine to serotype. In Western Paraná, S. agalactiae Ib is a major mortality driver, linked to septicemia and meningioencephalitis. Affected fish exhibit anorexia, lethargy, darkening, corneal opacity, exophthalmia, ascites, and disoriented or circular swimming; internal inflammation of heart and brain explains erratic movement and eye protrusion. Survivors may harbor lesions affecting processing quality. High disease recurrence after treatment complicates production. Francisella orientalis becomes more relevant in colder water (<24°C), reducing metabolism and feed intake and challenging oral treatments. Serotype Ib remains widely disseminated in the country; serotype III has re-emerged in the Southeast, including Triângulo Mineiro. Vaccination should be integrated with diagnostic effort, water quality management, and a sanitation calendar guided by water temperature, as discussed at SIMPOP in Toledo, Paraná.

articleHeadline: Does your cat go outside? An outbreak of sporotrichosis, a disease transmissible to humans, confirmed in Cascavel; see precautions.
articleSummary: Confirmed outbreak of sporotrichosis in cats in Cascavel, Paraná, Brazil, announced by the Cascavel Health Secretariat on August 19, 2026, with human transmission. Sporotrichosis is a fungal disease causing severe lesions in felines and can be fatal; human infection occurs through contact with wound secretions or bites or scratches from infected animals. First feline cases appeared in 2022, likely introduced by a roaming infected animal. The health division collects diagnostic samples, monitors treatment, and the city provides medications while conducting active searches for new foci. Residents are advised to seek medical evaluation for suspected infections. Veterinarians note the disease is treatable; do not abandon infected pets, isolate them, wear gloves and masks when handling wounds, and maintain hygiene with soap, water, and disinfectant. The Cascavel Hemocenter requests pet blood donors (phone 45 99132-4236). Donor criteria: cats 1–7 years, >4 kg, vaccinated, indoors; dogs 1–7 years, >25 kg, healthy, vaccinated, non-medicated, docile.

articleHeadline: Peptides advance against Salmonella as an alternative for ensuring food safety.
articleSummary: Brazilian HYH Biotechnology unveiled a platform of engineered antimicrobial peptides targeting Salmonella, with laboratory results showing initial control in about two hours and suppression of new colonies for more than four days. The platform was also evaluated against Escherichia coli and Listeria monocytogenes, achieving roughly 95% degradation of biofilms. Built from about four years of bioinformatics, computational modeling, peptide engineering, and validation, the approach uses multiple rationally designed peptides rather than a single molecule. Pending industrial validation, applications could span slaughterhouses, incubators, poultry farms, dairies, and egg-processing facilities in Brazil, aiming to strengthen hygiene, reduce cross-contamination and losses, and meet Brazilian and international market requirements. The technology is patent-protected and may form a base for multiple biosafety products. A cited study notes direct recall costs can reach US$10 million.

articleSummary: Tuberculosis awareness and prevention efforts were launched in Carapebus, Rio de Janeiro State, Brazil, by the Municipal Health Secretariat (Semsa). articleHeadline: Which countries are threatened by malaria-carrying mosquitoes?
articleSummary: As of 2026-08-19, Anopheles stephensi, a malaria-carrying mosquito native to South Asia, has expanded into Africa, first arriving via Eritrea and rapidly spreading to Ethiopia, Sudan, Somalia and Nigeria, with detections now in Ghana and Kenya. The spread threatens malaria control, placing more than 126 million people at risk. Unlike many local species, A. stephensi tolerates urban environments and breeds in artificial water containers, water tanks, construction debris, and discarded tires, allowing efficient transmission in crowded cities. It also shows high levels of resistance to many insecticides, complicating control efforts. WHO recommends a comprehensive, integrated vector management approach, including insecticide-treated nets and repellents for people, and elimination of standing water and other breeding sites. The situation highlights the urgent need for surveillance, vector control adaptation, and international cooperation to curb urban malaria expansion.
